"""
Monte Carlo mixture (unmixing) model.

Randomly weights the source samples, sums them into a model curve, scores that
against the sink, and keeps the best-scoring configurations.

Weights are drawn uniformly over every possible mixture (a flat Dirichlet), so
each configuration is a full partition of the sink and lopsided mixtures (one
source dominant, or one nearly absent) are tried as often as even ones.

With `refine=True` (the default) the best configurations are then polished by
constrained optimisation (SciPy's SLSQP, proportions in [0, 1] summing to 1),
as DZmix's default "minimum function search" and detritalPy do, and the single
best fit is the estimate. With `refine=False` the estimate is the mean of the
top configurations, as in the Monte Carlo model of Sundell & Saylor (2017).
Either way the spread of the top configurations is reported as the uncertainty.
"""
import numpy as np

from . import metrics

# metric -> (distribution form the metric expects, higher score is a better fit)
METRICS = {
    "cross_correlation": ("pdf", True),
    "likeness": ("pdf", True),
    "similarity": ("pdf", True),
    "ks": ("cdf", False),
    "kuiper": ("cdf", False),
}

DEFAULT_TRIALS = 10000
TOP_TRIALS = 10

# Trials are scored in blocks so peak memory stays bounded no matter how many
# bins the distributions have: a 10,000 x 2,000 model matrix would be 160 MB.
MAX_BLOCK_CELLS = 2_000_000


class Contribution:
    """One source's share of the sink, as a percentage."""

    def __init__(self, name: str, contribution: float, standard_deviation: float):
        self.name = name
        self.contribution = contribution
        self.standard_deviation = standard_deviation

    def __repr__(self):
        return (f"Contribution({self.name!r}, {self.contribution:.2f}%, "
                f"±{self.standard_deviation:.2f})")


class MixtureResult:
    """
    What one run of the model produced.

    Attributes:
        contributions - Contribution per source, in the order given
        top_lines     - (TOP_TRIALS, n_bins) model curves of the best trials;
                        when refined, the optimised best fit is the first
        top_scores    - the metric value for each of those curves
        metric        - the metric used
        refined       - whether the contributions are an optimised best fit
    """

    def __init__(self, contributions, top_lines, top_scores, metric,
                 grid_shape=None, refined=False):
        self.contributions = contributions
        self.top_lines = top_lines
        self.top_scores = top_scores
        self.metric = metric
        # True when contributions are an optimised best fit (whose curve and
        # score come first in top_lines / top_scores) rather than a trial mean.
        self.refined = refined
        # Set by the bivariate model: the (ny, nx) the flattened lines fold to.
        self.grid_shape = grid_shape

    @property
    def best_score(self):
        return float(self.top_scores[0]) if len(self.top_scores) else float("nan")

    @property
    def top_grids(self):
        """The winning trials folded back into density grids."""
        if not self.grid_shape:
            return []
        return [line.reshape(self.grid_shape) for line in self.top_lines]


def expected_form(metric: str) -> str:
    """Whether `metric` compares PDFs or CDFs."""
    try:
        return METRICS[metric][0]
    except KeyError:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown metric '{metric}'")


def higher_is_better(metric: str) -> bool:
    try:
        return METRICS[metric][1]
    except KeyError:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown metric '{metric}'")


def score_models(sink: np.ndarray, models: np.ndarray, metric: str) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Score every row of `models` against `sink`.

    Vectorized equivalents of sed_stats.metrics, which take one curve at a
    time; scoring 10,000 trials one call at a time is far too slow in the
    browser.
    """
    if metric == "ks":
        # metrics.ks: max absolute difference between the two curves
        return np.abs(models - sink).max(axis=1)

    if metric == "kuiper":
        # metrics.kuiper: max(sink - model) + max(model - sink)
        return (sink - models).max(axis=1) + (models - sink).max(axis=1)

    if metric == "cross_correlation":
        # metrics.r2: squared Pearson correlation
        centered_sink = sink - sink.mean()
        sink_energy = float(np.dot(centered_sink, centered_sink))
        centered = models - models.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
        numerator = centered @ centered_sink
        denominator = np.sqrt((centered * centered).sum(axis=1) * sink_energy)
        with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
            correlation = np.where(denominator > 0, numerator / denominator, np.nan)
        return correlation ** 2

    if metric == "similarity":
        # metrics.similarity: sum of sqrt(sink * model) (Gehrels, 2000); 1 = identical.
        return np.sqrt(np.clip(models, 0, None) * np.clip(sink, 0, None)).sum(axis=1)

    if metric == "likeness":
        # metrics.likeness: 1 - sum|sink - model| / 2 (Satkoski et al., 2013). For
        # distributions that each sum to 1 this is 1 - Bray-Curtis dissimilarity: the share of
        # the distribution the model already places correctly.
        return 1 - np.abs(models - sink).sum(axis=1) / 2

    raise ValueError(f"Unknown metric '{metric}'")


def random_configurations(n_trials: int, n_sources: int, rng) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    `n_trials` weight vectors, each non-negative and summing to 1, uniform over
    all such vectors.

    Normalizing independent uniforms instead would crowd the weights toward
    1/n: with 10 sources, only about 0.5% of configurations would give any
    source more than 30%, so a sink dominated by one source could not be found.
    """
    return rng.dirichlet(np.ones(n_sources), size=n_trials)


def _refine(starts, misfit):
    """
    The lowest-misfit weights found by SLSQP from each of `starts`.

    KS and Kuiper are maxima, so their misfit has many shallow local minima;
    starting from every top configuration, and from equal weights, and keeping
    the best end point makes the answer stable from run to run.
    """
    from scipy.optimize import minimize

    def objective(weights):
        value = misfit(weights)
        return value if np.isfinite(value) else 1e12

    n_sources = starts.shape[1]
    best, best_value = starts[0], objective(starts[0])
    for start in list(starts) + [np.full(n_sources, 1.0 / n_sources)]:
        found = minimize(objective, start, method="SLSQP",
                         bounds=[(0.0, 1.0)] * n_sources,
                         constraints={"type": "eq", "fun": lambda w: 1.0 - np.sum(w)},
                         options={"maxiter": 10000})
        weights = np.clip(found.x, 0.0, None)
        weights = weights / weights.sum()
        value = objective(weights)
        if value < best_value:
            best, best_value = weights, value
    return best


def _summarize(all_weights, all_scores, higher, n_top, source_matrix,
               score_one, source_names, metric, refine):
    """Rank the trials, optionally refine the winners, and build the result."""
    # A degenerate trial scores NaN; push those to the losing end rather than
    # letting argsort's NaN-last convention make them look like winners.
    ranked = np.where(np.isnan(all_scores),
                      -np.inf if higher else np.inf,
                      all_scores)
    order = np.argsort(ranked, kind="stable")
    top_indices = order[::-1][:n_top] if higher else order[:n_top]

    top_weights = all_weights[top_indices]
    top_scores = all_scores[top_indices]
    spread = top_weights.std(axis=0) * 100

    if refine:
        sign = -1.0 if higher else 1.0
        estimate = _refine(top_weights, lambda w: sign * score_one(w))
        # The optimised fit leads the bundle; the next-best trials follow it.
        line_weights = np.vstack([estimate, top_weights[1:]])
        top_scores = np.concatenate([[score_one(estimate)], top_scores[1:]])
    else:
        estimate = top_weights.mean(axis=0)
        line_weights = top_weights

    contributions = [
        Contribution(name, float(estimate[i] * 100), float(spread[i]))
        for i, name in enumerate(source_names)
    ]
    return MixtureResult(
        contributions=contributions,
        top_lines=line_weights @ source_matrix,
        top_scores=top_scores,
        metric=metric,
        refined=refine,
    )


def monte_carlo_model(sink_values, source_values, source_names=None,
                      n_trials: int = DEFAULT_TRIALS,
                      metric: str = "cross_correlation",
                      n_top: int = TOP_TRIALS,
                      seed=0,
                      refine: bool = True) -> MixtureResult:
    """
    Run the model.

    Args:
        sink_values: the sink sample's curve, as a 1-D array
        source_values: one curve per source, all on the sink's x grid
        source_names: labels for the sources; defaults to "Source 1", ...
        n_trials: how many random configurations to try
        metric: "cross_correlation", "likeness", "similarity", "ks", or "kuiper"
        n_top: how many of the best trials to keep (and average, if not refining)
        seed: fixed by default so rebuilding a figure reproduces its numbers;
              pass None for a fresh draw each run
        refine: polish the best trials by constrained optimisation and report
                the single best fit, rather than the mean of the top trials

    Raises:
        ValueError: on an unknown metric, no sources, or ragged inputs
    """
    if metric not in METRICS:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown metric '{metric}'")

    sink = np.asarray(sink_values, dtype=float)
    sources = np.asarray(source_values, dtype=float)
    if sources.ndim != 2 or sources.shape[0] == 0:
        raise ValueError("Need at least one source distribution")
    if sources.shape[1] != sink.shape[0]:
        raise ValueError("Sources and sink must share the same x grid")

    n_sources = sources.shape[0]
    if source_names is None:
        source_names = [f"Source {i + 1}" for i in range(n_sources)]

    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n_top = max(1, min(n_top, n_trials))

    # Only the weights and scores are kept for every trial; the model curves of
    # the winners are recomputed at the end from their weights.
    all_weights = np.empty((n_trials, n_sources))
    all_scores = np.empty(n_trials)

    block = max(1, min(n_trials, MAX_BLOCK_CELLS // max(sink.shape[0], 1)))
    for start in range(0, n_trials, block):
        stop = min(start + block, n_trials)
        weights = random_configurations(stop - start, n_sources, rng)
        all_weights[start:stop] = weights
        all_scores[start:stop] = score_models(sink, weights @ sources, metric)

    def score_one(weights):
        return float(score_models(sink, (weights @ sources)[None, :], metric)[0])

    return _summarize(all_weights, all_scores, higher_is_better(metric), n_top,
                      sources, score_one, source_names, metric, refine)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- bivariate

# The 2D measures of Sundell & Saylor (2021). Unlike the 1D table there is no
# "form" column: a bivariate distribution is always a density grid, and the
# CDF-based measures derive their own cumulative forms.
METRICS_2D = {
    "cross_correlation": True,   # higher is better
    "likeness": True,
    "similarity": True,
    "ks": False,
    "kuiper": False,
}


def _flatten_grid(distribution):
    """A BivariateDistribution or 2-D array as (densities, shape)."""
    grid = getattr(distribution, "densities", distribution)
    grid = np.asarray(grid, dtype=float)
    if grid.ndim != 2:
        raise ValueError("Expected a 2-D density grid")
    return grid.ravel(), grid.shape


def _quadrant_stack(grid):
    """Each of a grid's four quadrant CDFs, flattened into one row apiece."""
    from .distributions.bivariate import quadrant_cdfs

    return np.asarray([cdf.ravel() for cdf in quadrant_cdfs(grid)])


def _score_models_2d(sink_grid, sink_quadrants, source_flat, source_quadrants,
                     weights, metric):
    """Score a block of trials without ever materializing a per-trial cumsum."""
    models = weights @ source_flat

    if metric in ("cross_correlation", "likeness", "similarity"):
        # Both compare the flattened grids cell by cell (Sundell & Saylor 2021, eqs 17-18).
        return score_models(sink_grid, models, metric)

    # Cumulative summing is linear, so the quadrant CDF of a mixture is the
    # same mixture of the sources' quadrant CDFs. Precomputing them once turns
    # what would be four cumsums over the whole grid *per trial* into one more
    # matmul, which is what makes 2D unmixing affordable at all.
    best = None
    for quadrant in range(sink_quadrants.shape[0]):
        model_cdfs = weights @ source_quadrants[quadrant]
        difference = sink_quadrants[quadrant] - model_cdfs
        if metric == "ks":
            values = np.abs(difference).max(axis=1)
        else:  # kuiper
            values = difference.max(axis=1) + (-difference).max(axis=1)
        best = values if best is None else np.maximum(best, values)
    return best


def monte_carlo_model_2d(sink, sources, source_names=None,
                         n_trials: int = DEFAULT_TRIALS,
                         metric: str = "cross_correlation",
                         n_top: int = TOP_TRIALS,
                         seed=0,
                         refine: bool = True) -> MixtureResult:
    """
    Top-down unmixing on bivariate density grids.

    The same convex-mixture logic as the univariate model: a sink drawn from
    several source populations has a density that is a weighted sum of theirs,
    in two dimensions exactly as in one.

    K-S and Kuiper cannot be had by flattening the grid and running the 1D
    statistic — the cumulative sum would depend on whether you walked the grid
    by rows or by columns. They use the four quadrant CDFs of Peacock (1983)
    instead, as sed_stats.metrics_2d does.

    Args:
        sink: BivariateDistribution or 2-D array
        sources: one per source, all on the sink's grid
        source_names: labels; defaults to "Source 1", ...
        metric: "cross_correlation", "likeness", "similarity", "ks", or "kuiper"
        refine: polish the best trials by constrained optimisation (see
                monte_carlo_model)

    Returns:
        MixtureResult whose top_lines are flattened grids; use `.top_grids`
    """
    if metric not in METRICS_2D:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown metric '{metric}'")

    sink_flat, shape = _flatten_grid(sink)
    flattened = []
    for source in sources:
        source_flat, source_shape = _flatten_grid(source)
        if source_shape != shape:
            raise ValueError("Sources and sink must share the same grid")
        flattened.append(source_flat)
    if not flattened:
        raise ValueError("Need at least one source distribution")

    source_flat = np.asarray(flattened)
    n_sources = source_flat.shape[0]
    if source_names is None:
        source_names = [f"Source {i + 1}" for i in range(n_sources)]

    sink_quadrants = np.zeros((0, sink_flat.size))
    source_quadrants = np.zeros((0, n_sources, sink_flat.size))
    if metric in ("ks", "kuiper"):
        sink_quadrants = _quadrant_stack(sink_flat.reshape(shape))
        source_quadrants = np.stack(
            [_quadrant_stack(row.reshape(shape)) for row in source_flat], axis=1)

    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n_top = max(1, min(n_top, n_trials))

    all_weights = np.empty((n_trials, n_sources))
    all_scores = np.empty(n_trials)

    block = max(1, min(n_trials, MAX_BLOCK_CELLS // max(sink_flat.size, 1)))
    for start in range(0, n_trials, block):
        stop = min(start + block, n_trials)
        weights = random_configurations(stop - start, n_sources, rng)
        all_weights[start:stop] = weights
        all_scores[start:stop] = _score_models_2d(
            sink_flat, sink_quadrants, source_flat, source_quadrants,
            weights, metric)

    def score_one(weights):
        return float(_score_models_2d(sink_flat, sink_quadrants, source_flat,
                                      source_quadrants, weights[None, :], metric)[0])

    result = _summarize(all_weights, all_scores, METRICS_2D[metric], n_top,
                        source_flat, score_one, source_names, metric, refine)
    result.grid_shape = shape
    return result
scripts/sed_stats/niche.py:
"""
Isotopic niche: the standard ellipse and its area, the convex hull, and overlap.

After Jackson et al. (2011), J. Anim. Ecol. 80:595-602 (SIBER), whose definitions
were read from the paper:

  * the standard ellipse has the sample covariance matrix S for its shape, so its
    semi-axes are the square roots of S's eigenvalues, and its area (SEA) is
    pi * sqrt(det S). It is to a bivariate sample what the standard deviation is to
    a univariate one, and holds roughly 40 % of normally distributed points;
  * SEA is biased low for small samples, corrected by (n - 1) / (n - 2) (SEAc);
  * the total area (TA) is that of the convex hull of the points (Layman et al. 2007),
    which grows with every extra point, so it should not be compared between samples
    of different size.

Two further community measures from Layman et al. (2007) are given: the mean distance
to the centroid (CD) and the mean nearest-neighbour distance (MNND).
"""
import math

import numpy as np

from .hull import convex_hull

# A point cloud this small has no meaningful niche.
MINIMUM_POINTS = 3
# Below this, SEAc is available but is a poor estimate (Jackson et al. 2011 advise
# larger samples; Bayesian estimates are better for small n).
COMFORTABLE_POINTS = 10
SEGMENTS = 120


def _clean(xs, ys):
    pairs = [(float(x), float(y)) for x, y in zip(xs, ys)
             if x is not None and y is not None and math.isfinite(x) and math.isfinite(y)]
    return np.array([p[0] for p in pairs]), np.array([p[1] for p in pairs])


def covariance(xs, ys):
    """The 2 x 2 sample covariance matrix (n - 1 in the denominator)."""
    x, y = _clean(xs, ys)
    if len(x) < 2:
        raise ValueError("Need at least two points for a covariance.")
    return np.cov(np.vstack([x, y]))


def prediction_scale(level):
    """
    Factor on the standard ellipse's axes that makes it hold `level` (0-1) of
    bivariate-normal points: the square root of the chi-square quantile on two
    degrees of freedom, sqrt(-2 ln(1 - level)). 1 is the standard ellipse itself.
    """
    if not 0 < level < 1:
        raise ValueError("The share of points must be between 0 and 1.")
    return math.sqrt(-2.0 * math.log(1.0 - level))


def ellipse(xs, ys, scale=1.0, segments=SEGMENTS):
    """
    The vertices of the ellipse centred on the mean with the sample covariance's shape,
    its axes multiplied by `scale`. Empty if there are too few points or they lie on a line.
    """
    x, y = _clean(xs, ys)
    if len(x) < MINIMUM_POINTS:
        return []
    values, vectors = np.linalg.eigh(np.cov(np.vstack([x, y])))
    if values[0] <= 1e-12 * max(values[1], 1e-300):
        return []
    angle = np.linspace(0.0, 2.0 * math.pi, segments, endpoint=False)
    unit = np.vstack([np.cos(angle), np.sin(angle)])
    shape = vectors @ (np.sqrt(values)[:, None] * unit) * scale
    return [(float(x.mean() + a), float(y.mean() + b)) for a, b in zip(shape[0], shape[1])]


def polygon_area(vertices):
    """Shoelace area of a simple polygon."""
    if len(vertices) < 3:
        return 0.0
    v = np.array(vertices, dtype=float)
    return 0.5 * abs(float(np.dot(v[:, 0], np.roll(v[:, 1], -1))
                           - np.dot(v[:, 1], np.roll(v[:, 0], -1))))


def clip_convex(subject, clip):
    """
    The intersection of two convex polygons (Sutherland-Hodgman), counter-clockwise.
    Ellipses and hulls are convex, so this is exact for them.
    """
    def inside(p, a, b):
        return (b[0] - a[0]) * (p[1] - a[1]) - (b[1] - a[1]) * (p[0] - a[0]) >= 0

    def crossing(p, q, a, b):
        x1, y1, x2, y2 = p[0], p[1], q[0], q[1]
        x3, y3, x4, y4 = a[0], a[1], b[0], b[1]
        d = (x1 - x2) * (y3 - y4) - (y1 - y2) * (x3 - x4)
        t = ((x1 - x3) * (y3 - y4) - (y1 - y3) * (x3 - x4)) / d
        return (x1 + t * (x2 - x1), y1 + t * (y2 - y1))

    def counter_clockwise(poly):
        v = np.array(poly)
        signed = np.dot(v[:, 0], np.roll(v[:, 1], -1)) - np.dot(v[:, 1], np.roll(v[:, 0], -1))
        return list(poly) if signed >= 0 else list(reversed(poly))

    output = counter_clockwise(subject)
    clip = counter_clockwise(clip)
    for i in range(len(clip)):
        a, b = clip[i], clip[(i + 1) % len(clip)]
        points, output = output, []
        if not points:
            break
        previous = points[-1]
        for current in points:
            if inside(current, a, b):
                if not inside(previous, a, b):
                    output.append(crossing(previous, current, a, b))
                output.append(current)
            elif inside(previous, a, b):
                output.append(crossing(previous, current, a, b))
            previous = current
    return output


def overlap_area(first, second):
    """Area shared by two convex outlines (0 if either is empty or they do not meet)."""
    if len(first) < 3 or len(second) < 3:
        return 0.0
    return polygon_area(clip_convex(first, second))


def metrics(xs, ys):
    """
    The niche measures of one group, as a dict: n, mean x and y, sea, seac, ta, cd, mnnd.
    Areas are None where they cannot be found (too few points, or all on a line).
    """
    x, y = _clean(xs, ys)
    n = len(x)
    out = {"n": n, "mean_x": float(x.mean()) if n else None,
           "mean_y": float(y.mean()) if n else None,
           "sea": None, "seac": None, "ta": None, "cd": None, "mnnd": None}
    if n < MINIMUM_POINTS:
        return out
    determinant = float(np.linalg.det(np.cov(np.vstack([x, y]))))
    if determinant > 0:
        out["sea"] = math.pi * math.sqrt(determinant)
        out["seac"] = out["sea"] * (n - 1) / (n - 2)
    out["ta"] = polygon_area(convex_hull(x, y)) or None
    out["cd"] = float(np.mean(np.hypot(x - x.mean(), y - y.mean())))
    distances = np.hypot(x[:, None] - x[None, :], y[:, None] - y[None, :])
    np.fill_diagonal(distances, np.inf)
    out["mnnd"] = float(distances.min(axis=1).mean())
    return out
scripts/sed_stats/nmf.py:
"""
Non-negative matrix factorization of detrital geochronological data.

After Saylor, Sundell & Sharman (2019), "Characterizing sediment sources by
non-negative matrix factorization of detrital geochronological data", Earth and
Planetary Science Letters 512, 46-58.

The sink samples' distributions form a matrix V, one row per sample and one
column per bin of a shared grid. NMF finds sources H and weights W, all
non-negative, with V ~ W H: row i of W says how much of each source sample i
holds, and row j of H is source j's own distribution. The inversion is not unique
and wants more sink samples than sources, which `separability_warnings` checks.

What follows the paper:
    - V holds finite mixture distributions (PDPs or KDEs), never ECDFs.
    - The objective is the Euclidean distance, 1/2 ||V - W H||^2.
    - Each sample's weights sum to one and each source distribution sums to one.
    - The number of sources is the breakpoint of the final residual plotted against
      rank: two straight lines are fitted, one over the low ranks and one over the
      high, and the rank that minimises the sum of their squared residuals is chosen
      (`breakpoint_rank`).

What does not: the paper alternates non-negative least squares. This uses
hierarchical alternating least squares (Cichocki & Phan 2009), which minimises the
same objective by coordinate descent but is cheap enough to scan every rank in the
browser. Both reach stationary points of that objective from random starts; the
number of restarts, the stopping rule and the seed are this module's own choices.
"""
from dataclasses import dataclass

import numpy as np

EPS = 1e-12


@dataclass
class NMFResult:
    """
    Attributes:
        weights: (n_samples, rank) — each row sums to 1
        sources: (rank, n_bins) — each row sums to 1
        residual: the Frobenius norm of V - W H, after normalising
        rank: the number of sources
        iterations: iterations the best restart took
    """
    weights: np.ndarray
    sources: np.ndarray
    residual: float
    rank: int
    iterations: int = 0

    def reconstruction(self):
        return self.weights @ self.sources


def _hals(V, rank, rng, max_iter, tol):
    """One factorization from a random start; W and H unnormalised."""
    n, m = V.shape
    scale = np.sqrt(max(V.mean(), EPS) / rank)
    W = rng.random((n, rank)) * scale + EPS
    H = rng.random((rank, m)) * scale + EPS
    previous = np.inf
    iteration = 0
    for iteration in range(1, max_iter + 1):
        # H, one source at a time, against the current weights.
        WtV, WtW = W.T @ V, W.T @ W
        for j in range(rank):
            if WtW[j, j] < EPS:                     # a source that died: restart it
                H[j] = rng.random(m) * scale + EPS
                continue
            H[j] = np.maximum(
                EPS, H[j] + (WtV[j] - WtW[j] @ H) / WtW[j, j])
        # Then W, one source at a time, against the new sources.
        VHt, HHt = V @ H.T, H @ H.T
        for j in range(rank):
            if HHt[j, j] < EPS:
                continue
            W[:, j] = np.maximum(
                EPS, W[:, j] + (VHt[:, j] - W @ HHt[:, j]) / HHt[j, j])
        error = np.linalg.norm(V - W @ H)
        if previous - error <= tol * max(previous, EPS) and iteration > 5:
            break
        previous = error
    return W, H, iteration


def _normalise(W, H):
    """Sources that sum to one, weights that sum to one, reconstruction kept."""
    scale = H.sum(axis=1)
    scale[scale < EPS] = 1.0
    H = H / scale[:, None]
    W = W * scale[None, :]
    totals = W.sum(axis=1)
    totals[totals < EPS] = 1.0
    return W / totals[:, None], H


def factorize(V, rank, restarts=10, max_iter=500, tol=1e-7, seed=0):
    """
    Factorize V into `rank` sources, keeping the best of several random starts.

    Args:
        V: (n_samples, n_bins) non-negative, each row a distribution
        rank: number of sources, at least 1 and at most the number of samples
        restarts: random starts; the lowest final residual wins
        seed: fixes the starts, so the same data gives the same answer

    Raises:
        ValueError: for a rank that cannot be fitted, or negative data
    """
    V = np.asarray(V, dtype=float)
    if V.ndim != 2 or V.size == 0:
        raise ValueError("The data must be a samples-by-bins table.")
    if (V < 0).any():
        raise ValueError("NMF needs non-negative data.")
    if not 1 <= rank <= V.shape[0]:
        raise ValueError(f"The number of sources must be between 1 and the number "
                         f"of samples ({V.shape[0]}).")
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    best = None
    for _ in range(max(1, restarts)):
        W, H, iterations = _hals(V, rank, rng, max_iter, tol)
        W, H = _normalise(W, H)
        residual = float(np.linalg.norm(V - W @ H))
        if best is None or residual < best.residual:
            best = NMFResult(W, H, residual, rank, iterations)
    return best


def scan_ranks(V, ranks, **kwargs):
    """{rank: NMFResult} for each rank, for choosing how many sources there are."""
    return {rank: factorize(V, rank, **kwargs) for rank in ranks}


def _line_ssr(x, y):
    """Squared residual of the least-squares line through the points (0 for two or fewer)."""
    if len(x) <= 2:
        return 0.0
    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
    return float(np.sum((y - (slope * x + intercept)) ** 2))


def breakpoint_rank(ranks, residuals):
    """
    The number of sources, from how the final residual falls with rank.

    The residual drops quickly until the true number of sources is reached and
    slowly after. Two straight lines are fitted — one over the ranks up to a
    candidate breakpoint and one from it onwards, each by least squares — and the
    candidate with the smallest total squared residual is the rank.

    Returns:
        (rank, totals): the chosen rank, and the summed squared residuals for
        every candidate, in the order of `ranks`

    Raises:
        ValueError: with fewer than three ranks, where there is no curve to bend
    """
    x = np.asarray(ranks, dtype=float)
    y = np.asarray(residuals, dtype=float)
    if len(x) < 3 or len(x) != len(y):
        raise ValueError("Choosing the number of sources needs at least three ranks.")
    totals = [_line_ssr(x[:i + 1], y[:i + 1]) + _line_ssr(x[i:], y[i:])
              for i in range(len(x))]
    return int(x[int(np.argmin(totals))]), totals


def fit_quality(V, result):
    """R^2 between each sample's distribution and its reconstruction (Pearson, as
    the paper's cross-correlation)."""
    rebuilt = result.reconstruction()
    out = []
    for observed, modelled in zip(np.asarray(V, float), rebuilt):
        if observed.std() < EPS or modelled.std() < EPS:
            out.append(float("nan"))
        else:
            out.append(float(np.corrcoef(observed, modelled)[0, 1] ** 2))
    return out


def separability_warnings(V, rank):
    """
    The paper's conditions for trusting a factorization, as plain sentences for
    whichever are not met. Its simulations found sources recovered well when there
    were more than about three times as many sink samples as sources, and the
    sinks differed from one another (their cross-correlation coefficients spanning
    more than 0.3).
    """
    V = np.asarray(V, dtype=float)
    notes = []
    samples = V.shape[0]
    if samples < 3 * rank:
        notes.append(
            f"{samples} samples is fewer than three times {rank} sources. In "
            "Saylor et al.'s tests sources were recovered reliably only with more "
            "than about three times as many sink samples as sources.")
    if samples >= 3:
        r2 = np.corrcoef(V) ** 2
        pairs = r2[np.triu_indices(samples, k=1)]
        pairs = pairs[~np.isnan(pairs)]
        if pairs.size and pairs.max() - pairs.min() < 0.3:
            notes.append(
                "The samples are very alike (their cross-correlation spans "
                f"{pairs.max() - pairs.min():.2f}, under 0.3), which makes the "
                "sources poorly constrained.")
    return notes
scripts/sed_stats/pca.py:
"""
Principal component analysis over per-sample distributions.

Each sample is one observation and every grid position is a feature, so a set
of distributions becomes an (n_samples, n_points) matrix. The first two
components are the plane that captures the most variance between samples.

This is the linear counterpart to sed_stats.mds: MDS starts from a pairwise
dissimilarity matrix and only preserves rank order or distance, whereas PCA
works on the distributions themselves and so can also report *which* parts of
the distribution drive the separation, via the component loadings.

Computation only — plotting is left to the caller.
"""
import numpy as np


class PCAPoint:
    """One sample's position in component space."""

    def __init__(self, x: float, y: float, label: str):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y
        self.label = label

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"PCAPoint({self.label!r}, {self.x:.4g}, {self.y:.4g})"


class PCAResult:
    """
    Attributes:
        points          - PCAPoint per sample, in the order given
        scores          - (n_samples, n_components) coordinates
        components      - (n_components, n_features) loadings, one row per PC
        explained_ratio - fraction of total variance per component
        mean            - the feature mean that was subtracted
        singular_values - from the SVD, for a scree plot
    """

    def __init__(self, points, scores, components, explained_ratio, mean,
                 singular_values, explained_ratio_all=None, blocks=None):
        self.points = points
        self.scores = scores
        self.components = components
        self.explained_ratio = explained_ratio
        self.mean = mean
        self.singular_values = singular_values
        # Every component, not just the kept ones — a scree plot needs the tail
        # to show where the useful variance stops.
        self.explained_ratio_all = (explained_ratio if explained_ratio_all is None
                                    else explained_ratio_all)
        # [(variable_name, start, stop), ...] when the feature vector was
        # concatenated from several variables; empty for a single-variable PCA.
        self.blocks = blocks or []

    def percent(self, component: int) -> float:
        """Percent of variance explained by a 0-indexed component."""
        if component >= self.explained_ratio.size:
            return 0.0
        return float(self.explained_ratio[component] * 100)

    def block_contributions(self, component: int):
        """
        How much each variable drives a component, as fractions summing to 1.

        Only meaningful for a combined_pca result. Component rows are unit
        vectors, so the squared loadings inside one variable's slice are that
        variable's share of the component.

        Returns:
            [(name, fraction), ...], or [] when the PCA was over one variable
        """
        if not self.blocks or component >= self.components.shape[0]:
            return []
        loadings = self.components[component] ** 2
        total = float(loadings.sum()) or 1.0
        return [(name, float(loadings[start:stop].sum()) / total)
                for name, start, stop in self.blocks]


class GrainPCAResult:
    """
    A PCA fitted across individual measurements rather than whole samples.

    Attributes:
        scores          - (n_grains, n_components) per-grain coordinates
        components      - (n_components, n_variables) loadings
        explained_ratio - fraction of total variance per component
        variables       - the variable names, in column order
        mean, scale     - the standardization that was applied
    """

    def __init__(self, scores, components, explained_ratio, variables,
                 mean, scale, explained_ratio_all=None):
        self.scores = scores
        self.components = components
        self.explained_ratio = explained_ratio
        self.variables = list(variables)
        self.mean = mean
        self.scale = scale
        self.explained_ratio_all = (explained_ratio if explained_ratio_all is None
                                    else explained_ratio_all)

    def percent(self, component: int) -> float:
        if component >= self.explained_ratio.size:
            return 0.0
        return float(self.explained_ratio[component] * 100)

    def loadings(self, component: int):
        """[(variable, loading), ...] for one component, largest first."""
        if component >= self.components.shape[0]:
            return []
        pairs = list(zip(self.variables, self.components[component]))
        return sorted(pairs, key=lambda pair: abs(pair[1]), reverse=True)


def grain_pca(matrix, variables=None, n_components: int = 2,
              weights=None, column_weights=None) -> GrainPCAResult:
    """
    Fit one PCA across every measurement, for use as a derived axis.

    This is the transform that makes multivariate top-down unmixing work. A
    mixture of grain populations produces a distribution that is a convex
    combination of its sources' distributions, and that stays true under any
    fixed per-grain map — so projecting every grain onto a single, globally
    fitted PC1 gives a new scalar whose distributions still mix linearly.

    Two things it therefore must NOT do, both of which would break that
    property: fit separately per sample, or standardize per sample. The fit and
    the standardization are global, over the pooled measurements.

    Args:
        matrix: (n_grains, n_variables), every grain from every sample
        variables: column names, for reporting the loadings
        n_components: how many components to keep
        weights: optional per-grain weight. Pass 1/n for each grain of a
            sample to stop a sample with many analyses from dominating the
            axis; the projection itself stays unweighted.
        column_weights: optional per-variable multiplier applied after
            standardizing. A categorical variable one-hot encoded into k
            columns would otherwise outweigh a numeric one k to 1; giving each
            of its columns 1/sqrt(k) makes the whole block count as one
            variable.

    Raises:
        ValueError: with fewer than two grains or fewer than two variables
    """
    matrix = np.asarray(matrix, dtype=float)
    if matrix.ndim != 2:
        raise ValueError("Expected a (grains, variables) matrix")
    n_grains, n_variables = matrix.shape
    if n_grains < 2:
        raise ValueError("Need at least two measurements")
    if n_variables < 2:
        raise ValueError("Need at least two variables")

    if variables is None:
        variables = [f"v{i + 1}" for i in range(n_variables)]

    if weights is None:
        weight_vector = np.ones(n_grains)
    else:
        weight_vector = np.asarray(weights, dtype=float)
        if weight_vector.shape[0] != n_grains:
            raise ValueError("weights must be one per measurement")
    total_weight = float(weight_vector.sum()) or 1.0

    mean = (weight_vector @ matrix) / total_weight
    centered = matrix - mean

    # Standardize: variables in different units (Ma, °C, ratios) would
    # otherwise be ranked by the size of their numbers, not their information.
    variance = (weight_vector @ (centered ** 2)) / total_weight
    scale = np.sqrt(variance)
    scale[scale <= 0] = 1.0  # a constant column carries nothing either way
    standardized = centered / scale
    if column_weights is not None:
        column_weights = np.asarray(column_weights, dtype=float)
        if column_weights.shape[0] != n_variables:
            raise ValueError("column_weights must be one per variable")
        standardized = standardized * column_weights

    # The SVD is weighted; the projection is not, so every grain still lands at
    # its own honest position on the axis.
    weighted = standardized * np.sqrt(weight_vector)[:, np.newaxis]
    _, singular_values, right = np.linalg.svd(weighted, full_matrices=False)

    n_components = max(1, min(n_components, n_variables))
    components = right[:n_components].copy()
    scores = standardized @ components.T
    components, scores = _flip_signs(components, scores)

    total = float(np.sum(singular_values ** 2))
    explained_ratio = (singular_values ** 2 / total) if total > 0 else \
        np.zeros_like(singular_values)

    return GrainPCAResult(
        scores=scores,
        components=components,
        explained_ratio=explained_ratio[:n_components],
        explained_ratio_all=explained_ratio,
        variables=variables,
        mean=mean,
        scale=scale,
    )


def _flip_signs(components, scores):
    """
    Pin the arbitrary sign of each component.

    An SVD is only defined up to a sign per component, so an unpinned plot can
    come out mirrored for no reason. Forcing the largest-magnitude loading
    positive makes the orientation reproducible.
    """
    for i in range(components.shape[0]):
        largest = int(np.argmax(np.abs(components[i])))
        if components[i, largest] < 0:
            components[i] *= -1
            scores[:, i] *= -1
    return components, scores


def _decompose(centered, sample_names, mean, n_components, blocks=None) -> PCAResult:
    """The shared SVD core, on an already-centered matrix."""
    n_samples, n_features = centered.shape
    # An n-sample set spans at most n-1 dimensions once it is centered.
    n_components = max(1, min(n_components, n_samples - 1, n_features))

    # SVD rather than an eigendecomposition of the covariance matrix: there are
    # far more grid points than samples, so the covariance matrix would be huge
    # and rank-deficient.
    _, singular_values, right = np.linalg.svd(centered, full_matrices=False)

    components = right[:n_components].copy()
    scores = centered @ components.T
    components, scores = _flip_signs(components, scores)

    total = float(np.sum(singular_values ** 2))
    explained_ratio = (singular_values ** 2 / total) if total > 0 else \
        np.zeros_like(singular_values)

    points = [
        PCAPoint(float(scores[i, 0]),
                 float(scores[i, 1]) if n_components > 1 else 0.0,
                 name)
        for i, name in enumerate(sample_names)
    ]

    return PCAResult(
        points=points,
        scores=scores,
        components=components,
        explained_ratio=explained_ratio[:n_components],
        explained_ratio_all=explained_ratio,
        mean=mean,
        singular_values=singular_values,
        blocks=blocks,
    )


def pca_function(series, n_components: int = 2) -> PCAResult:
    """
    Run PCA on a list of (sample_name, values) pairs.

    Args:
        series: every sample's distribution, all on the same grid
        n_components: how many components to keep

    Returns:
        PCAResult

    Raises:
        ValueError: with fewer than two samples, or ragged distributions
    """
    if len(series) < 2:
        raise ValueError("PCA needs at least two samples")

    matrix = np.asarray([np.asarray(values, dtype=float) for _, values in series])
    if matrix.ndim != 2:
        raise ValueError("Every sample must be on the same grid")

    mean = matrix.mean(axis=0)
    return _decompose(matrix - mean, [name for name, _ in series], mean,
                      n_components)


def clr(matrix):
    """
    Centered log-ratio of rows of proportions.

    Shares that sum to 1 carry one fewer degree of freedom than they have
    entries, and an abundant category swamps a plain PCA. The log-ratio frees
    them from the constant sum and works in relative terms. Zeros have no
    logarithm, so each is replaced by half the smallest positive share before
    the rows are renormalized.

    Args:
        matrix: (n_samples, n_categories), each row summing to 1

    Raises:
        ValueError: if no entry is positive
    """
    shares = np.asarray(matrix, dtype=float)
    positive = shares[shares > 0]
    if positive.size == 0:
        raise ValueError("Need at least one positive share")
    shares = np.where(shares > 0, shares, positive.min() / 2)
    shares = shares / shares.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    logs = np.log(shares)
    return logs - logs.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)


def combined_pca(blocks, sample_names, n_components: int = 2,
                 weighting: str = "equal") -> PCAResult:
    """
    One PCA over several variables at once.

    Each sample's feature vector is its distribution for every variable laid
    end to end, so the result answers "how do these samples relate given
    everything measured" rather than one variable at a time.

    Args:
        blocks: [(variable_name, matrix)], each matrix (n_samples, n_features_i)
                with rows in the same sample order
        sample_names: one per row, shared by every block
        n_components: how many components to keep
        weighting: "equal" divides each variable by its own first singular
                   value, so a variable cannot dominate merely by having a
                   longer grid or larger numbers (Escofier & Pages' multiple
                   factor analysis). "none" concatenates raw.

    Raises:
        ValueError: with no blocks, fewer than two samples, or mismatched rows
    """
    if not blocks:
        raise ValueError("Need at least one variable")
    if len(sample_names) < 2:
        raise ValueError("PCA needs at least two samples")

    pieces = []
    spans = []
    start = 0
    for name, matrix in blocks:
        matrix = np.asarray(matrix, dtype=float)
        if matrix.shape[0] != len(sample_names):
            raise ValueError(f"'{name}' has {matrix.shape[0]} rows, "
                             f"expected {len(sample_names)}")
        centered = matrix - matrix.mean(axis=0)

        scale = 1.0
        if weighting == "equal":
            values = np.linalg.svd(centered, compute_uv=False)
            if values.size and values[0] > 0:
                scale = float(values[0])

        pieces.append(centered / scale)
        spans.append((name, start, start + centered.shape[1]))
        start += centered.shape[1]

    # Every block was centered on its own, so the concatenation already is.
    combined = np.hstack(pieces)
    return _decompose(combined, list(sample_names),
                      np.zeros(combined.shape[1]), n_components, blocks=spans)
scripts/sed_stats/regression.py:
"""
Straight-line fits of one variable on another, for lines such as a local meteoric
water line (delta-2H against delta-18O).

Either can be weighted, by precipitation amount for a local meteoric water line: the weighted
fit minimises sum(w * residual^2) with each point's weight w (Hughes & Crawford 2012, who
weighted by rainfall amount; Crawford et al. 2014 compared the weighted and unweighted forms of
these methods). Large events then count for more, and the many small ones, whose d-excess is
often lowered by evaporation below the cloud, for less.

Two methods, both defined by their formulas:
  * ordinary least squares, y on x: the slope is cov(x, y) / var(x). It treats x as
    exact and puts all the scatter in y;
  * reduced major axis, which treats the two alike: |slope| = sd(y) / sd(x), with the
    sign of the correlation. Where both variables are measured with error (as isotope
    ratios are) it is the usual alternative, and for a high correlation the two agree.
"""
import math

import numpy as np

METHODS = {"ols": "Ordinary least squares (y on x)", "rma": "Reduced major axis"}


def linear_fit(xs, ys, method="ols", weights=None):
    """
    Fit y = slope * x + intercept.

    Args:
        weights: a weight for each point (an amount), or None for equal weights. Only their
            ratios matter: multiplying every weight by a constant changes nothing. A point
            with a missing or zero weight is left out.

    Returns:
        dict: n, slope, intercept, r2, slope_se, intercept_se (the standard errors of
        the least squares fit, which are the ones in common use, for either method;
        weighted, they use sum(w * r^2) / (n - 2) for the variance), x_min, x_max, weighted

    Raises:
        ValueError: for fewer than three points, x with no spread, a negative weight, or an
            unknown method
    """
    if method not in METHODS:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown method '{method}'.")
    if weights is None:
        weights = [1.0] * len(xs)
    if len(weights) != len(xs):
        raise ValueError("Each point needs a weight.")
    weighted = any(w != weights[0] for w in weights)
    pairs = []
    for x, y, w in zip(xs, ys, weights):
        if x is None or y is None or w is None:
            continue
        x, y, w = float(x), float(y), float(w)
        if not (math.isfinite(x) and math.isfinite(y) and math.isfinite(w)):
            continue
        if w < 0:
            raise ValueError("A weight cannot be negative.")
        if w > 0:
            pairs.append((x, y, w))
    if len(pairs) < 3:
        raise ValueError("Need at least three points to fit a line.")
    x = np.array([p[0] for p in pairs])
    y = np.array([p[1] for p in pairs])
    w = np.array([p[2] for p in pairs])
    n = len(x)
    total = w.sum()
    mx, my = float((w * x).sum() / total), float((w * y).sum() / total)
    sxx = float((w * (x - mx) ** 2).sum())
    syy = float((w * (y - my) ** 2).sum())
    sxy = float((w * (x - mx) * (y - my)).sum())
    if sxx <= 0:
        raise ValueError("The x values do not vary, so no line can be fitted.")
    r = sxy / math.sqrt(sxx * syy) if syy > 0 else 0.0
    ols_slope = sxy / sxx
    ols_intercept = my - ols_slope * mx
    residual = float((w * (y - (ols_slope * x + ols_intercept)) ** 2).sum())
    mean_square = residual / (n - 2)
    slope_se = math.sqrt(mean_square / sxx)
    intercept_se = math.sqrt(mean_square * (1.0 / total + mx ** 2 / sxx))
    if method == "rma":
        if syy <= 0:
            raise ValueError("The y values do not vary, so no line can be fitted.")
        slope = math.copysign(math.sqrt(syy / sxx), sxy)
        intercept = my - slope * mx
    else:
        slope, intercept = ols_slope, ols_intercept
    return {"n": n, "slope": slope, "intercept": intercept, "r2": r * r,
            "slope_se": slope_se, "intercept_se": intercept_se,
            "x_min": float(x.min()), "x_max": float(x.max()), "weighted": weighted}

"""
Multidimensional scaling by majorization, and the isotonic fit it needs.

These replace scikit-learn's `manifold.MDS` and `isotonic.IsotonicRegression`.
Not for want of trust in those — they are the reference this was checked
against — but for weight: scikit-learn drags SciPy behind it, and the pair
costs about 19 MB of the roughly 22 MB this app downloads before it can run.
Two algorithms of a hundred lines each is a fair trade for that.

SMACOF (Scaling by MAjorizing A COmplicated Function, de Leeuw 1977) minimises
Kruskal's raw stress

    sigma(X) = sum over i<j of (d_ij(X) - dhat_ij)^2

by repeatedly applying the Guttman transform, which is guaranteed not to
increase the stress. In metric MDS the target dhat is the dissimilarity
itself; in non-metric MDS it is whatever monotonically increasing function of
the dissimilarities best fits the current distances — which is what the
isotonic regression supplies.
"""
import numpy as np


def isotonic_regression(x, y, weights=None) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Fit a non-decreasing step function of `x` to `y`, by least squares.

    Pool Adjacent Violators: walk the points in order of `x` keeping a stack
    of blocks, and whenever a new block's mean falls below its predecessor's
    merge the two. Merging can cascade, but each point joins and leaves a
    block at most once, so the whole pass is linear.

    Ties in `x` are averaged before fitting. Without that, two points sharing
    an x could be given different fitted values, and the result would not be a
    function of x at all.

    Returns:
        Fitted values, in the order the inputs were given.
    """
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
    if x.shape != y.shape:
        raise ValueError("x and y must be the same length")
    if x.size == 0:
        return np.array([], dtype=float)

    w = np.ones(x.size) if weights is None else np.asarray(weights, dtype=float)

    # Stable sort, so equal x keep their input order and group together.
    order = np.argsort(x, kind="mergesort")
    x_sorted, y_sorted, w_sorted = x[order], y[order], w[order]

    # Collapse ties into one weighted point each. reduceat rather than a
    # comprehension over np.split: non-metric SMACOF calls this once per
    # iteration per restart, so it is genuinely hot.
    starts = np.concatenate(([0], np.flatnonzero(np.diff(x_sorted)) + 1))
    sizes = np.diff(np.append(starts, x_sorted.size))
    group_weight = np.add.reduceat(w_sorted, starts)
    weighted = np.add.reduceat(w_sorted * y_sorted, starts)
    group_value = np.where(group_weight > 0,
                           weighted / np.where(group_weight > 0, group_weight, 1),
                           np.add.reduceat(y_sorted, starts) / sizes)

    # PAVA over the collapsed points.
    value = np.empty(group_value.size)
    weight = np.empty(group_value.size)
    count = np.empty(group_value.size, dtype=int)
    top = 0
    for index in range(group_value.size):
        value[top] = group_value[index]
        weight[top] = group_weight[index]
        count[top] = 1
        while top > 0 and value[top - 1] > value[top]:
            combined = weight[top - 1] + weight[top]
            value[top - 1] = (
                (weight[top - 1] * value[top - 1] + weight[top] * value[top])
                / combined if combined > 0
                else (value[top - 1] + value[top]) / 2
            )
            weight[top - 1] = combined
            count[top - 1] += count[top]
            top -= 1
        top += 1

    # Back out to every original point: block value -> group -> input order.
    per_group = np.repeat(value[:top], count[:top])
    fitted = np.empty(x.size)
    fitted[order] = np.repeat(per_group, sizes)
    return fitted


def _pairwise_distances(points: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Euclidean distance matrix, with an exact zero diagonal."""
    squared = np.sum(points ** 2, axis=1)
    gram = points @ points.T
    distances = squared[:, None] + squared[None, :] - 2 * gram
    np.maximum(distances, 0, out=distances)
    np.sqrt(distances, out=distances)
    np.fill_diagonal(distances, 0.0)
    return distances


def classical_mds(dissimilarities: np.ndarray, n_components: int = 2) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Torgerson scaling: an eigen-decomposition that lands near the answer.

    Used as SMACOF's starting point. A random start needs many restarts to
    avoid a poor local minimum; starting from the classical solution usually
    converges to a better one, and does so in the same place every time.
    """
    n = dissimilarities.shape[0]
    squared = dissimilarities ** 2
    # Double centering turns squared distances into a Gram matrix.
    centering = np.eye(n) - np.ones((n, n)) / n
    gram = -0.5 * centering @ squared @ centering
    gram = (gram + gram.T) / 2  # symmetrize away the rounding

    values, vectors = np.linalg.eigh(gram)
    # eigh returns ascending; the largest eigenvalues carry the structure.
    order = np.argsort(values)[::-1][:n_components]
    values, vectors = values[order], vectors[:, order]
    return vectors * np.sqrt(np.maximum(values, 0))


def _stress_1(distances, fitted) -> float:
    """
    Kruskal's stress-1: the residual, normalised by the distances themselves.

    Scale-invariant, which raw stress is not — and in non-metric MDS the
    configuration's overall size is free, so raw stress cannot be compared
    between runs at all. A configuration collapsing toward a point would post
    a flatteringly small raw stress while fitting nothing.
    """
    total = float(np.sum(distances ** 2))
    if total <= 0:
        return 1.0  # everything on top of everything: the worst possible fit
    return float(np.sqrt(np.sum((distances - fitted) ** 2) / total))


def _smacof_single(dissimilarities, n_components, metric, max_iter, eps,
                   init=None, rng=None):
    """One SMACOF run. Returns (embedding, stress-1, iterations)."""
    n = dissimilarities.shape[0]
    upper = np.triu_indices(n, k=1)
    delta = dissimilarities[upper]

    if init is not None:
        points = np.array(init, dtype=float)
    else:
        points = rng.uniform(-1.0, 1.0, size=(n, n_components))

    target = np.empty((n, n))
    previous = None
    stress = 0.0
    iteration = 0

    for iteration in range(1, max_iter + 1):
        distance_matrix = _pairwise_distances(points)
        distances = distance_matrix[upper]

        if metric:
            fitted = delta
        else:
            # The monotone transform of the dissimilarities that best matches
            # the current distances, rescaled to fix the arbitrary overall
            # size that a rank-only target would otherwise leave free.
            fitted = isotonic_regression(delta, distances)
            norm = np.sqrt(np.sum(fitted ** 2))
            if norm > 0:
                fitted = fitted * np.sqrt(fitted.size) / norm

        stress = float(np.sum((distances - fitted) ** 2))
        normalized_stress = _stress_1(distances, fitted)

        # Guttman transform. Zero distances would divide by zero; they also
        # contribute nothing, so their ratio is pinned to zero.
        target[upper] = fitted
        target.T[upper] = fitted
        np.fill_diagonal(target, 0.0)

        with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
            ratio = np.where(distance_matrix > 0, target / distance_matrix, 0.0)
        guttman = -ratio
        np.fill_diagonal(guttman, 0.0)
        np.fill_diagonal(guttman, -guttman.sum(axis=1))
        points = (guttman @ points) / n

        # Convergence on the stress relative to the configuration's own size,
        # so the test does not depend on how large the numbers happen to be.
        scale = np.sum(np.sqrt(np.sum(points ** 2, axis=1)))
        normalized = stress / scale if scale > 0 else stress
        if previous is not None and abs(previous - normalized) < eps:
            break
        previous = normalized

    return points, normalized_stress, iteration


def smacof(dissimilarities, n_components: int = 2, metric: bool = True,
           n_init: int = 8, max_iter: int = 300, eps: float = 1e-6,
           random_state: int = 0):
    """
    Fit an embedding to a precomputed dissimilarity matrix.

    The first run starts from the classical MDS solution, which is
    deterministic and usually good; the rest start randomly, in case that one
    sits in a poor local minimum. The lowest-stress run wins.

    Args:
        dissimilarities: symmetric (n, n), zero diagonal
        metric: True preserves distances, False only their rank order
        n_init: how many starts to try
        random_state: pinned, so the same data always gives the same map

    Returns:
        (embedding, stress_1) where embedding is (n, n_components) and
        stress_1 is Kruskal's normalised stress — scale-invariant, so it is
        comparable between runs and between datasets.
    """
    dissimilarities = np.asarray(dissimilarities, dtype=float)
    n = dissimilarities.shape[0]
    if dissimilarities.ndim != 2 or dissimilarities.shape[1] != n:
        raise ValueError("dissimilarities must be a square matrix")
    if n <= n_components:
        # Fewer points than dimensions: the classical solution is exact.
        return classical_mds(dissimilarities, n_components), 0.0

    rng = np.random.default_rng(random_state)

    best_points, best_stress = None, np.inf
    for run in range(max(1, n_init)):
        init = classical_mds(dissimilarities, n_components) if run == 0 else None
        points, stress, _ = _smacof_single(
            dissimilarities, n_components, metric, max_iter, eps,
            init=init, rng=rng)
        # Compared on stress-1, never raw stress: see _stress_1.
        if stress < best_stress:
            best_points, best_stress = points, stress

    return best_points, float(best_stress)
scripts/sed_stats/ternary.py:
"""
Ternary (three-component) compositions.

A ternary plot shows three parts of a whole — QFL modal counts, a
clay/silt/sand split, three normalized oxides. Each grain is one point, and
because the three parts sum to a constant the point has only two degrees of
freedom, which is what lets a triangle hold it without loss.

Two things follow from "sums to a constant" and both are handled here:

  * Raw measurements rarely sum to exactly 100. Point counts stop at whatever
    total the operator counted to; percentages carry rounding. Closing each
    row to a constant sum is the standard first step, not a fudge.
  * A composition that sums to zero has no position on the triangle at all,
    and a negative part has none either. Those rows are reported rather than
    silently plotted somewhere wrong.
"""
import numpy as np

# Apex order, and what each position means. Plotly names them a/b/c; the
# geological convention puts the first at the top and reads the other two
# left to right along the base.
APEX_KEYS = ("a", "b", "c")
APEX_POSITIONS = ("top", "lower left", "lower right")

DEFAULT_TOTAL = 100.0

# How far a row's raw sum may sit from the target before it is worth
# mentioning — a percent either way is rounding, more than that is a
# different scale or a missing component.
CLOSURE_TOLERANCE = 1.0


class TernaryData:
    """
    Three components closed to a constant sum, plus what had to be dropped.

    Attributes:
        a, b, c   - the closed components, each (n,), summing row-wise to total
        total     - the constant they sum to
        keep      - boolean mask of the input rows that survived
        raw_sums  - each surviving row's sum before closure
        dropped   - {"nonpositive": n, "negative": n} counts of what was removed
    """

    def __init__(self, a, b, c, total, keep, raw_sums, dropped):
        self.a = a
        self.b = b
        self.c = c
        self.total = total
        self.keep = keep
        self.raw_sums = raw_sums
        self.dropped = dropped

    def __len__(self):
        return int(self.a.size)

    @property
    def dropped_total(self):
        return sum(self.dropped.values())

    @property
    def needed_closure(self):
        """Whether any surviving row's raw sum was far enough off to mention."""
        if self.raw_sums.size == 0:
            return False
        return bool(np.abs(self.raw_sums - self.total).max() > CLOSURE_TOLERANCE)

    @property
    def closure_range(self):
        """(min, max) of the raw row sums, for reporting what was normalized."""
        if self.raw_sums.size == 0:
            return (0.0, 0.0)
        return (float(self.raw_sums.min()), float(self.raw_sums.max()))


def close(a, b, c, total: float = DEFAULT_TOTAL) -> TernaryData:
    """
    Scale each row so its three parts sum to `total`.

    "Closure" is the compositional-data term for this: only the ratios between
    the parts carry information, so rescaling a row to a common sum discards
    nothing and makes rows comparable.

    Rows with a negative part, or with all three parts at zero, are dropped —
    neither has a position on the triangle.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if the three inputs are not the same length
    """
    a = np.asarray(a, dtype=float)
    b = np.asarray(b, dtype=float)
    c = np.asarray(c, dtype=float)
    if not (a.shape == b.shape == c.shape):
        raise ValueError("The three components must be the same length")

    stacked = np.vstack([a, b, c])
    finite = np.isfinite(stacked).all(axis=0)
    negative = finite & (stacked < 0).any(axis=0)
    sums = stacked.sum(axis=0)
    nonpositive = finite & ~negative & (sums <= 0)

    keep = finite & ~negative & ~nonpositive
    kept = stacked[:, keep]
    raw_sums = kept.sum(axis=0)
    closed = kept / raw_sums * total

    return TernaryData(
        a=closed[0], b=closed[1], c=closed[2], total=float(total),
        keep=keep, raw_sums=raw_sums,
        dropped={
            "negative": int(negative.sum()),
            "nonpositive": int(nonpositive.sum()),
            "missing": int((~finite).sum()),
        },
    )


def to_cartesian(a, b, c, total: float = DEFAULT_TOTAL):
    """
    Triangle coordinates as (x, y), for anything that needs a flat plane.

    The `a` apex sits at the top, `b` at the lower left and `c` at the lower
    right, matching APEX_POSITIONS. Plotly draws ternary traces from a/b/c
    directly, so this is for the computations that need a metric — nearest
    neighbours, a density, a convex hull.
    """
    a = np.asarray(a, dtype=float) / total
    b = np.asarray(b, dtype=float) / total
    c = np.asarray(c, dtype=float) / total
    return 0.5 * (2 * c + a), (np.sqrt(3) / 2) * a


def centroid(data: TernaryData):
    """
    The mean composition, as an (a, b, c) triple on the same scale.

    Arithmetic rather than geometric: the geometric (Aitchison) centre is the
    better-founded average for compositional data, but it is undefined when
    any part is exactly zero, which is common in modal counts — a sandstone
    with no lithics is an ordinary observation, not a missing one.
    """
    if not len(data):
        return (float("nan"),) * 3
    return (float(data.a.mean()), float(data.b.mean()), float(data.c.mean()))
scripts/sed_stats/thiem.py:
"""
Steady-state drawdown to a pumping well in a confined aquifer: the Thiem equation.

    s(r) = Q · ln(R / r) / (2π · K · b)          (any consistent units)

the drawdown s at distance r from a well pumping Q from an aquifer of hydraulic conductivity K
and thickness b, when the cone of depression reaches a radius R (the radius of influence, where
drawdown is zero). K · b is the transmissivity T. The drawdown is logarithmic in distance, so it
is a straight line on a semilog plot, and the contours round a single well are circles whose
radii are r = R · exp(-s · 2π K b / Q).

Two sets of units are offered:

  "us"  Q in gpm, lengths in feet, K in gpd/ft². Written as in Driscoll (1986, p. 214) and the
        usual hydrogeology course:   s = 528 · Q · log10(R / r) / (K · b).  The 528 is the
        conversion (1,440 min/day ÷ 2π, times ln 10 ≈ 527.7) rounded as the textbook rounds it.
  "si"  Q in m³/day, lengths in metres, K in m/day, with the equation exactly as above.

Assumptions of the equation itself: a confined aquifer of uniform thickness, homogeneous and
isotropic, a fully penetrating well, steady flow, and no regional gradient (a sloping water
table or potentiometric surface is ignored). It does not apply as it stands to an unconfined
aquifer, where the drawdown is a sizeable fraction of the saturated thickness, or to flow that
is still changing (that is the Theis equation).
"""
import math

UNITS = {
    "us": {"label": "US (gpm, ft, gpd/ft²)", "flow": "gpm", "length": "ft", "k": "gpd/ft²"},
    "si": {"label": "SI (m³/day, m, m/day)", "flow": "m³/day", "length": "m", "k": "m/day"},
}

# s = FACTOR * Q * log10(R / r) / (K * b)
FACTOR = {"us": 528.0, "si": math.log(10.0) / (2.0 * math.pi)}


def _factor(units):
    if units not in FACTOR:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown units '{units}'.")
    return FACTOR[units]


def _check(**values):
    for name, value in values.items():
        if value is None or not math.isfinite(value) or value <= 0:
            raise ValueError(f"{name} must be a number above zero.")


def conductivity(flow, thickness, radius_of_influence, well_radius, drawdown_at_well, units="us"):
    """
    Hydraulic conductivity from the drawdown measured in the pumping well itself (the first
    question of the usual problem set).

    Raises:
        ValueError: for a non-positive input, or a radius of influence not beyond the well
    """
    _check(flow=flow, thickness=thickness, radius_of_influence=radius_of_influence,
           well_radius=well_radius, drawdown_at_well=drawdown_at_well)
    if radius_of_influence <= well_radius:
        raise ValueError("The radius of influence must be larger than the well's radius.")
    return (_factor(units) * flow * math.log10(radius_of_influence / well_radius)
            / (thickness * drawdown_at_well))


def drawdown(distance, flow, conductivity_, thickness, radius_of_influence, well_radius=None,
             units="us"):
    """
    Drawdown at `distance` from the well (a number or a NumPy array). Beyond the radius of
    influence it is zero; closer than the well's radius it is the drawdown at the well's wall.
    """
    import numpy as np
    _check(flow=flow, conductivity=conductivity_, thickness=thickness,
           radius_of_influence=radius_of_influence)
    r = np.asarray(distance, dtype=float)
    if well_radius is not None:
        r = np.maximum(r, well_radius)
    if np.any(r <= 0):
        raise ValueError("Distances from the well must be above zero.")
    s = _factor(units) * flow * np.log10(radius_of_influence / r) / (conductivity_ * thickness)
    s = np.maximum(s, 0.0)
    return float(s) if s.ndim == 0 else s


def distance_for_drawdown(level, flow, conductivity_, thickness, radius_of_influence, units="us"):
    """The distance from the well at which the drawdown is `level` (the radius of that contour)."""
    _check(level=level, flow=flow, conductivity=conductivity_, thickness=thickness,
           radius_of_influence=radius_of_influence)
    return radius_of_influence * 10.0 ** (-level * conductivity_ * thickness
                                          / (_factor(units) * flow))


def contour_radii(interval, flow, conductivity_, thickness, radius_of_influence, well_radius,
                  units="us"):
    """
    [(level, radius)] for the contours at every `interval` of drawdown that lie in the aquifer,
    that is, between the well's wall and the radius of influence. A level at or above the
    drawdown in the well itself is inside the well and has no contour.
    """
    _check(interval=interval)
    wall = drawdown(well_radius, flow, conductivity_, thickness, radius_of_influence, units=units)
    found, k = [], 1
    while k * interval <= wall + 1e-9 and k < 500:
        level = k * interval
        found.append((level, distance_for_drawdown(level, flow, conductivity_, thickness,
                                                   radius_of_influence, units)))
        k += 1
    return found


def transmissivity(conductivity_, thickness):
    """T = K · b, in the units of K times the units of b."""
    return conductivity_ * thickness


def parse_distances(text):
    """
    Distances typed as "200, 600" (commas, spaces or semicolons) as floats, in the order
    given.

    Raises:
        ValueError: naming the entry that is not a positive number
    """
    found = []
    for token in str(text or "").replace(";", ",").replace("\n", ",").split(","):
        for piece in token.split():
            try:
                value = float(piece)
            except ValueError:
                raise ValueError(f"'{piece}' is not a distance.") from None
            if not math.isfinite(value) or value <= 0:
                raise ValueError(f"'{piece}' is not a distance above zero.")
            found.append(value)
    return found

"""
Antioch Demo Splash Screen

This splash screen displays while Pyodide loads, providing SEO-friendly
static HTML content for search engines and a better user experience.
"""

from antioch.static import StaticPage, Div, P, keyframe, rotate, opacity, translateY

# Sky-strata-sky: blue fading to the icon's own sky color, a thin band of the
# strata browns across the middle, then back out to blue.
DEEP_BLUE = "#305a88"
SKY_BLUE = "#99b1cb"  # sampled from assets/sed_stats.png
STRATA = ["#ccc3ba", "#b2a48a", "#9c8969", "#9e6549", "#8e5b42", "#665141"]

BAND_START, BAND_END = 35, 65

# The sky reaches full light blue this far short of the band, leaving a stretch
# for it to wash into the first brown instead of meeting it at a hard edge.
BLEND = 5


def strata_gradient(angle="135deg"):
    """The background gradient, with the browns held to the middle band."""
    span = BAND_END - BAND_START
    stops = [f"{DEEP_BLUE} 0%", f"{SKY_BLUE} {BAND_START - BLEND}%"]
    for i, color in enumerate(STRATA):
        position = BAND_START + span * i / (len(STRATA) - 1)
        stops.append(f"{color} {position:g}%")
    stops.append(f"{SKY_BLUE} {BAND_END + BLEND}%")
    stops.append(f"{DEEP_BLUE} 100%")
    return f"linear-gradient({angle}, {', '.join(stops)})"


# Define keyframe animations pythonically!
@keyframe
def spin():
    rotate({0: 0, 100: 360})


@keyframe
def fadeInDown():
    opacity({0: 0, 100: 1})
    translateY({0: -30, 100: 0})


@keyframe
def fadeInUp():
    opacity({0: 0, 100: 1})
    translateY({0: 30, 100: 0})


def generate_splash():
    """Generate the static splash screen HTML."""

    # Create the page with SEO metadata
    page = StaticPage(title="Sed/Stats", lang="en")
    page.set_title("Sed/Stats")
    page.add_meta(
        name="viewport",
        content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0, maximum-scale=1.0, user-scalable=no"
    )

    # SEO Meta Tags
    page.set_description(
        "Sed/Stats is a web app that facilitates visualization and interpretation of sedimentological data"
        "Upload your data and generate high-quality, publication-ready figures in just a few clicks."
    )
    page.set_keywords("sedimentology", "geology", "detrital zircon", "python", "mixture modeling", "microplastics")
    page.set_author("Ryan Nielsen")

    # Open Graph tags for social media
    page.set_og_title("Sed/Stats")
    page.set_og_description("Build publication-ready figures in just a few clicks")
    page.set_og_url("https://sedstats.com")

    # Add animations to page
    page.add_style(spin.render())
    page.add_style(fadeInDown.render())
    page.add_style(fadeInUp.render())

    # Set body styles using dictionary assignment (just like DOM.body.style in Antioch!)
    page_div = Div(style = {
        'margin': '0',
        'padding': '0',
        'font_family': '-apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", Roboto, "Helvetica Neue", Arial, sans-serif',
        'background': strata_gradient(),
        'min_height': '100vh',
        'display': 'flex',
        'justify_content': 'center',
        'align_items': 'center',
        'color': 'white'
    })


    # Build the splash screen content with pythonic styles
    container = Div(id="loading-splash", style={
        'text-align': 'center',
        'padding': '40px',
        'max-width': '600px'
    })

    # Logo with gradient text effect
    logo = Div("Sed/Stats", style={
        'font-size': '4em',
        'font-weight': 'bold',
        'margin-bottom': '20px',
        'background': 'linear-gradient(135deg, #fff 0%, #f0f0f0 100%)',
        '-webkit-background-clip': 'text',
        '-webkit-text-fill-color': 'transparent',
        'background-clip': 'text'
    })

    # Tagline
    tagline = P("Visualize and Interpret Sedimentological Data", style={
        'font-size': '1.5em',
        'margin-bottom': '30px',
        'opacity': '0.9',
        'animation': 'fadeInUp 0.8s ease-out 0.2s both'
    })

    # Spinner
    spinner_container = Div(style={
        'margin': '30px auto 20px auto',
        'animation': 'fadeInUp 0.8s ease-out 0.6s both'
    })
    spinner = Div(style={
        'border': '4px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.3)',
        'border-top': '4px solid white',
        'border-radius': '50%',
        'width': '60px',
        'height': '60px',
        'animation': 'spin 1s linear infinite',
        'margin': '0 auto'
    })
    spinner_container.add(spinner)

    # Loading text
    loading_text = P("Loading modules...", style={
        'font-size': '1.1em',
        'margin': '0',
        'opacity': '0.8'
    })

    # Add all elements to container
    container.add(logo, tagline, spinner_container, loading_text)
    page_div.add(container)
    page.add(page_div)

    return page


# Allow running this file directly to preview the splash screen
if __name__ == "__main__":
    import sys
    from pathlib import Path

    # Add parent directory to path to import antioch.static
    sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).parent.parent))

    page = generate_splash()
    preview_path = Path(__file__).parent.parent / "splash_preview.html"

    with open(preview_path, "w") as f:
        f.write(page.render())

    print(f"✅ Splash screen preview saved to: {preview_path}")
    print(f"   Open it in a browser to see how it looks!")
